title: The Afternoon Brief: Energy crisis escalates as inflation data forces Fed decision
dek: Oil crossed $107 a barrel as Houthi forces seized Red Sea chokepoints, while August inflation surprised higher on energy costs. The Federal Reserve faces a rate decision next week as central banks globally signal tighter policy to combat conflict-driven price pressures.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Middle East escalation has created a dual constraint on policymakers: oil prices at multi-year highs are driving inflation that demands rate increases, but tighter policy risks slowing an economy already pressured by rising energy costs across goods, food, and transportation.
bottom_line: Oil breached $107 on Houthi territorial gains in the Red Sea while August inflation surprised higher on energy costs, forcing the Federal Reserve's hand at next week's meeting. The ECB already raised rates and warned inflation will persist into 2027; markets now price a 90 percent chance of a Fed hike. The honest read: energy supply constraints are real, not speculative, and central banks are locked into tightening policy even as that policy risks slowing growth. Watch the Fed's September 16-17 decision and whether oil prices hold above $100 through the midterms; either outcome will reshape the political and economic landscape entering the final eight weeks of the campaign.
body: The day's through-line is inescapable: oil-driven inflation is narrowing the options for central banks and governments. Energy markets, geopolitics, and monetary policy have fused into a single problem.

The Energy Cascade. Crude oil jumped to $107-108 per barrel today, driven by Houthi seizures of the strategic Red Sea positions of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on September 10-11. The strait, at its narrowest 19 miles across, controls roughly 12 percent of global seaborne trade. Diesel prices hit a record $6.05 per gallon this morning, up 60 percent from a year ago. Brent crude is now up roughly 20 percent since mid-August and 6 percent since yesterday, as the Houthis' advance signals sustained disruption to global shipping. British natural gas prices rose above 203 pence per therm, the highest since December 2022, and the Dutch wholesale gas price hit 82.56 euros per megawatt hour. These are not marginal moves.

Inflation Arrives Faster Than Expected. The August consumer price index released this morning showed headline inflation held at 3.4 percent annually, but core inflation, the figure that excludes volatile energy and food, rose to 2.4 percent, an upside surprise. Gasoline accounted for more than one-third of the month's overall price increase. Food prices rose modestly overall, but meat, poultry, eggs, and dairy all climbed between 0.1 and 0.3 percent. Shelter costs ticked up 0.3 percent. Technology and communications prices posted their largest yearly increase on record, with computer software up 25.4 percent annually. Real average hourly earnings declined 0.1 percent from July to August. Households are losing purchasing power in real terms even as headline inflation holds.

Central Banks Lock In Tighter Policy. The European Central Bank raised its main interest rate to 2.5 percent on September 10, its highest level since March 2025, and ECB President Christine Lagarde warned that inflation will not return to target until the end of 2027 due to Middle East conflict. The statement explicitly framed the conflict as a structural driver, not a temporary shock. Global government bond yields spiked in response. The 30-year German bond yield rose 2.5 basis points to 5.08 percent, the highest since December 2003. The UK 10-year yield surpassed 5.37 percent, the highest since 2007. U.S. Treasury yields also climbed sharply. Market odds for a Federal Reserve rate hike at next week's meeting jumped from under 70 percent to nearly 90 percent immediately after the inflation data released this morning. Odds for an October hike rose to almost 60 percent. The Fed faces a choice: validate market expectations with a rate increase that risks slowing growth, or hold and signal it sees the energy shock as temporary, a call that would likely trigger another bond sell-off.

Why This Moment Matters. The Houthi seizures of Mokha and Perim Island end a four-year truce and place Iran-backed forces within striking range of one of the world's two most critical oil chokepoints. EU gas storage sits at 67 percent capacity, well below the five-year average of 84 percent. The supply picture is genuinely constrained. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have reduced refining capacity globally, amplifying price pressures for diesel and gasoline. Freight costs, which account for 15 to 30 percent of total food costs, are climbing. Analysts warn that if diesel prices remain elevated beyond six weeks, the cost will begin trickling down to grocery shelves, transportation, furniture, and any good that moves by truck or ship. The supply-side shocks are real and layered.

The Political Cross-Current. President Trump told the Republican Midterm Convention on September 9 that the Iran war will end "very shortly after the election," linking a military conflict to electoral outcomes rather than military or diplomatic progress. NBC News polling shows 69 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the war. Yet primary elections this week showed voter anger focused on local governance: Helena Foulkes defeated incumbent Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee by running on the bridge closure that has paralyzed commutes for three years; David Morales, a 27-year-old democratic socialist, defeated Providence's incumbent mayor Brett Smiley by running on rent caps after Smiley vetoed a rent-stabilization ordinance. The pattern is clear: voters are punishing incumbents for failures in their direct experience, traffic, housing, local services, not responding to national messaging about the economy or foreign policy.

The Fed's Narrow Path. The central bank meets Tuesday and Wednesday, September 16-17. The core inflation surprise this morning, combined with the ECB's explicit signal that it is tightening policy, leaves the Fed with limited room to hold rates. A hold would require the Fed to signal it sees the energy shock as temporary; a hike validates market expectations and the narrative of persistent conflict-driven inflation. Whichever path it chooses, it will signal something about whether it believes the Houthi advances and Middle East escalation represent a structural shift in energy supply or a temporary disruption that will resolve by year-end. Oil prices remaining at or above $100 through November's midterm elections will test Trump's post-election resolution forecast and the Fed's confidence in a soft landing.
